blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Multilingual benchmarks for African languages mostly translate generic questions into local languages, measuring linguistic competence but not whether models know facts about Africa. We introduce \naija, a benchmark of factual and statistical questions about Nigeria, authored by native speakers and grounded in authoritative official statistics, with every question available in English, Nigerian Pidgin, \yoruba, Igbo, and Hausa. Answering similar questions for the UK and US yields a country by language matrix that disentangles a language effect (the model knows the fact but degrades in a low-resource language) from a knowledge effect (the fact is absent in every language). Across eight frontier and Nigeria-adapted models, the knowledge effect dominates: English-query accuracy is 49--50\% for the US/UK but 20\% for Nigeria. The language effect is smaller and tracks web representation, degrading from English to \yoruba{} (9 points on Nigeria, up to 24 on US/UK questions). We find scale does not help: the strongest models reach 66--79\% on the UK and the US but none exceed 31\% on Nigerian statistics. Extending to all 54 African countries with our best performing frontier model shows the same profile continent-wide, 96\% on culture and 98\% on politics against 26\% on statistics, so the gap is not specific to Nigeria.

blocks.en: 1 Introduction
blocks.zh: 导言

blocks.en:
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as sources of factual
information, yet their factual reliability is uneven and hard to
audit [ 24 , 29 ] . The problem compounds for
low-resource languages and for facts about under-represented regions. The
languages spoken across Nigeria illustrate the gap. As
Figure 1 shows, they are spoken by tens to hundreds of
millions of people, yet occupy a small share of the digital text on
which models are pretrained. A model can therefore fail on a Nigerian fact for
two different reasons: because it cannot process the language, or because
the fact was never well represented in its training data. Existing multilingual
benchmarks for African languages, such as AfriQA [ 22 ] ,
AfroBench [ 23 ] , and
IrokoBench/AfriMMLU [ 1 ] , largely evaluate models
by translating generic questions into African languages, which does not isolate
whether a model holds grounded knowledge about Africa itself.

blocks.en:
We introduce NaijaFacts, a benchmark of 100 factual questions about national
demographic and health statistics, authored by native speakers of the Nigerian
languages and translated to English. Its ground truth is authoritative,
quantitative official statistics, primarily demographic and health indicators
from bodies such as the National Population Commission (NPC), the National
Bureau of Statistics (NBS), and the Nigeria Demographic and Health Survey
(NDHS). Each question is available in English, Nigerian Pidgin, Yorùbá, Igbo, and Hausa, and is asked about three countries, giving 1,500 graded items per model. By holding the fact fixed and varying only the language of the query, NaijaFacts separates the language and knowledge effects.

blocks.en:
We make three contributions. First, we build a benchmark that pairs
official-statistic ground truth with five-language coverage and a country × \times language design, which separates the language and knowledge failure
modes. Second, we show that the knowledge effect dominates: eight models,
spanning three geopolitical origins and including two Nigeria-adapted 8B
open-weight models, hold UK and US statistics far better than Nigerian ones, and
answering in English recovers almost nothing. Third, we extend the construction
to all 54 African countries, which shows where the deficit generalises and which
facts escape it.

blocks.zh: 2 相关工作

blocks.en:
Work outside the Africa-focused research has varied the query language and the subject, but separately. Varying the query language, X-FACTR [ 11 ] and mLAMA [ 13 ] probe entity-level facts with cloze prompts, Qi et al. [25] show that scale improves per-language accuracy but
not cross-language consistency, and Aggarwal et al. [2] find on 10,000
country-related facts in 13 languages that a model can recall a fact in one
language and fail on it in another. Varying the subject instead,
WorldBench [ 16 ] asks the same World Bank indicator questions
about different countries and finds sizeable geographic disparities, while
PopQA [ 15 ] and Head-to-Tail [ 26 ] show
recall drops sharply for entities that are less popular online.

blocks.en: 3 The NaijaFacts Benchmark
blocks.zh: 3 奈哈事实基准

blocks.en:
NaijaFacts puts 1,500 graded items to every model: 100 factual questions about
national demographic and health statistics, each posed in five languages and
asked about three countries, Nigeria, the United Kingdom and the United States.
The questions are authored in the Nigerian languages, not translated into them,
and every answer comes from authoritative official statistics. Because each
country is asked the same question, a difference between countries reflects the
answer, not question difficulty or phrasing. That is what separates a language
effect from a knowledge effect.

each question into English, and we review it, giving five renderings per
question. We lightly edit questions so each is self-contained and answerable for
a given country.

blocks.en: 3.2 Ground truth
blocks.zh: 3.2 事实真相

blocks.en:
For every question we collect a gold answer for each of the three countries.
For Nigeria, the native speakers who authored the questions also provide the
answers in the Nigerian languages, grounded in the official national statistics
of the National Population Commission (NPC), National Bureau of Statistics
(NBS), and Nigeria Demographic and Health Survey (NDHS). For the United Kingdom and the United States, where these speakers are not the
domain authority, we obtain answers differently. A deep-research assistant
retrieves the relevant figure from official statistics, the Office for National
Statistics for the UK and the U.S. Census Bureau for the US. The four native
speakers who authored the questions then verify and correct each one. Grounding
answers in official statistics gives unambiguous, citable ground truth, and for
the UK/US answers retrieving the figure before writing it minimises fabrication.
Every item records the body, release and reference year behind its answer, and
those years span 2006 to 2025. Table 8 breaks the items down by
source.

blocks.en: 3.4 Extension to 54 countries
blocks.zh: 3.4 扩大到54个国家

blocks.en:
To test whether the Nigeria results are idiosyncratic, we reuse the same recipe
to build an English-only set for every African country. Each country gets
118–125 verified items built to a fixed blueprint, which holds the domain mix
and answer-type distribution constant so that countries stay comparable. Every
answer comes from that country’s own record. Statistical values are fetched
programmatically from the World Bank World Development Indicators and the DHS
Program APIs, never transcribed by a model, so a numeric gold answer cannot be
hallucinated and verifying one is simply a re-fetch. Items whose value is
missing or ambiguous at fetch time are dropped, which is why the per-country
count varies. Because instruments genuinely disagree, each indicator is pinned
to a single instrument across all countries. This yields 6,689 items spanning

blocks.en: 4 Experimental Setup
blocks.zh: 4 实验设置

blocks.en:
We evaluate eight models (Table 5 , Appendix E ): six frontier models
spanning three geopolitical origins (US, EU, CN), and two Nigeria-adapted
open-weight models, N-ATLaS and AfroLlama-V1, both 8B Llama-3 fine-tunes that
test whether targeted language adaptation helps. Frontier models are accessed
through AWS Bedrock; the 8B models run locally on a single 24 GB GPU. All models share one harness and identical prompts, with a 4,096-token answer budget. Sampling is left at each provider’s default for the hosted models, because Claude Opus 5 rejects an explicit temperature or top- p p ; the two local open-weight models are sampled at temperature 0.1.

blocks.en:
The mainline condition is native: each question is asked in the target
language and answered in that language, as a speaker would actually use the

expression failures. For the country analysis, each question explicitly names
the country it concerns (with a country-specific analog where a direct swap
would be unnatural) and is scored against that country’s gold answer, yielding
the country × \times language matrix of Section 5 .

blocks.en:
The knowledge effect dominates the language effect.
Even in English, the best model reaches only 29% on Nigerian statistics, while
the same three strongest models score 66–79% on the matched US and UK sets.
Averaged over models, the English-language gap
between the US/UK and Nigeria is 30 points (Table 6 ), more
than three times the largest language effect on the Nigeria set. Most failures on Nigerian facts are
therefore not translation failures: the fact is absent in every language.
This inverts the ordering Tonja et al. [27] report for African
cultural knowledge, where the language effect is the larger of the two, and the
domain is what differs. Everyday culture is well represented in web text, so
what remains to be lost there is expression, while the statistical record is
largely absent, so language has little left to subtract.

同样三个最强的模型在对等的美国和英国的赛事中得分为66-79%.

blocks.en:
Adaptation to Nigerian languages does not supply Nigerian knowledge.
The Nigeria-adapted 8B models score 6–15% (N-ATLaS) and 0–11%
(AfroLlama-V1), which is unsurprising at 30 to 100 times fewer parameters. They
also degrade across languages in the same direction and by much the same
proportion: the mean relative drop from English to Yorùbá is 51% for them
against 50% for the frontier models. N-ATLaS is the more stable of the two: its coefficient of variation across the
five languages is 34% against AfroLlama-V1’s 68%. The most stable models overall
are the strongest frontier ones (Claude Opus 5 10%, GPT-5.6 13%, Grok 4.6 15%). Both adapted
models are weakest in Igbo, but only one of them lacks Igbo adaptation.
AfroLlama-V1 was never trained for it, its card listing Swahili, Xhosa, Zulu,
Yorùbá, Hausa and English [ 10 ] , so its 0% there is
unsurprising. N-ATLaS was: its card reports roughly 200,000 Igbo
instruction samples, the same budget as Hausa and Yorùbá, and its developers’
own human evaluation rates its Igbo output above its
Yorùbá [ 3 ] . Yet its factual accuracy is lowest in Igbo at 6%
and twice that in Hausa at 12%, so equal adaptation data and better-rated
fluency did not translate into better factual recall. Fine-tuning
an 8B model on Nigerian languages therefore leaves both gaps open at this
scale: it neither supplies the factual record nor buys robustness to the query
language. Closing the factual gap appears to need frontier scale or explicit
injection of African knowledge during training.

blocks.en:
If a model knows a fact but cannot express it in Yorùbá, letting it answer in
English should recover the accuracy. We re-ran the full Nigeria set with
questions still asked in each Nigerian language but answers requested in

model that fails on a Nigerian fact asked in Yorùbá does not know the fact,
and is not merely unable to say it in Yorùbá. If translation were the problem,
removing it would have recovered the accuracy. Figure 6 compares
the two conditions per model.

A similar asymmetry has been measured outside Africa.
LocalBench [ 9 ] reports 56.8% on narrative questions about
US counties against under 15.5% on numerical ones, so part of what we see is a
general difficulty with quantitative facts and not specific to Africa. It cannot
be the whole story, though, because the UK and US sets beat every African country
on comparable facts. Both effects are present, and the geographic one survives
after the numeric one is accounted for.

blocks.en:
We think the explanation is the form in which these statistics exist, not whether
they exist at all. Every figure we grade is public, but it lives inside a PDF
report table, and pretraining corpora are dominated by running prose, so a number
can be openly available and still barely present in what a model absorbs. That
would explain why contamination looks unlikely even though every source is open,
and it predicts which fix works: retrieval over authoritative tables rather than
more pretraining.

blocks.en: 7 Conclusion
blocks.zh: 7 结论

blocks.en:
NaijaFacts is a multilingual benchmark that grounds factual questions about
Nigeria in authoritative official statistics and separates two failure modes
that translation-based benchmarks conflate: degradation in a low-resource
language, and absence of the underlying fact. Asking the same questions about
the UK and the US separates country familiarity from language resource level.

Naija Facts是一个多语种基准,它为事实问题提供了依据。
尼日利亚在权威官方统计中,将两种失败模式分开
基于翻译的基准将:低资源退化
语言,和缺乏基本事实。 问同样的问题
联合王国和美国将熟悉国家的情况与语言资源水平分开。

blocks.en:
The knowledge effect dominates. Asked in English, models average 49–50% on US
and UK official statistics but only 20% on the matched Nigerian statistics, and
answering in English recovers essentially nothing, so most failures on Nigerian
facts reflect missing knowledge and not translation. Scale does not rescue it
either: the strongest models reach 66–79% on the UK and US sets while no model
exceeds 31% on Nigerian statistics. The language effect is real but smaller and
tracks web representation, falling from English through Pidgin, Hausa, and Igbo
to Yorùbá, and it costs most where models have knowledge to lose. Across all 54
African countries the profile is the same, with 96% accuracy on culture and
98% on politics against 26% on official statistics.

超过31%的尼日利亚统计数据。 语言效果是真实的,但较小
由英语从Pidgin、Hausa和Igbo流出
给Yorúbá, 并且它花费最大 在模型有 知识损失。 所有54个
非洲国家的概况相同,对文化和农业的准确度为96%。
98%在政治方面,26%在官方统计方面。

blocks.en:
Serving African users therefore needs authoritative African data, the
statistical record in particular, curated into training corpora, not only
models adapted to African languages. We release the data, harness, and per-item
outputs so the benchmark can be reproduced and extended to further countries.
blocks.zh:
因此,为非洲用户服务需要权威的非洲数据,即:
特别是统计记录,编入培训公司,不仅
适应非洲语言的模式。 我们发布数据,使用,和每个项目
因此,基准可以复制并扩大到更多国家。

blocks.en:
Our study has a few limitations that future work should address.

The Nigeria subset is 100 items per language drawn largely from a few source
tables, so it probes grounded statistical knowledge and not broad knowledge, and
the 54-country extension is English-only on a single model. Official statistics
are also public, so contamination cannot be excluded, though the low accuracy on
statistics suggests these tables are poorly absorbed in practice. The next steps
follow: extending the multilingual design beyond Nigeria, and testing whether
injecting statistical tables during training moves the number that language
adaptation leaves fixed.
